Reasoning surface

Paths in Polynomial Lemniscates: Proofs and Examples

Erdős #1041

The short note centres on the trinomial identity in Section . That proof does not use Newton flow. The area-growth comparison is proved here in Section . The other constructions are independent of that proof. This record provides their derivations and keeps failed estimates beside the witnesses that refute them.

The historical question

Problem 1.1 (Erdős #1041). Let f(z)=∏i=1n(z−zi)f(z)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(z-z_i) be monic of degree n≥2n\ge2, with zi∈𝔻z_i\in\mathbb{D}, the open unit disc. Must two of the roots be joined by a curve of length less than 22 lying in the open lemniscate {z∈ℂ:|f(z)|<1}\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|f(z)|<1\}?

The open-disc hypothesis is essential for this formulation. For f(z)=z2−1f(z)=z^2-1, whose roots lie on the unit circle, every continuous path from −1-1 to 11 meets the imaginary axis. There |f(iy)|=1+y2≥1|f(iy)|=1+y^2\ge1, so no such path lies in the open unit lemniscate. Repeated roots, counted as distinct occurrences, give a constant path; the substantive case is therefore squarefree.

The problem numbering follows Bloom’s Erdős problem catalogue . A degree-seven counterexample due to the erdosproblems.com contributor ani makes the unrestricted total-variation assertion false. For one explicit monic polynomial of degree seven whose roots are distinct and lie in the open unit disc, every continuous path in the strict unit lemniscate joining two distinct roots has total variation greater than 22.1 Thus this polynomial has no continuous root-to-root parametrisation of total variation less than 22. The original source is Problem 5 on printed p. 139 of Erdős–Herzog–Piranian [4]; the preceding paragraph records the known input that one component of the lemniscate contains at least two zeros.

The main constructions use different kinds of information. The trinomial identity controls a prescribed path directly. The area argument instead uses the number of roots in a sublevel component. Source comparisons for component counts and lemniscate topology accompany the inverse-sheet discussion in Section ; the Newton-flow terminology is introduced in Section .

Two recent manuscripts are relevant. The 48-page manuscript posted by shtuka on 24 March 2026 [10] claims the unrestricted statement. Its Proposition 12 (p. 16, with proof continuing through p. 30) supplies the spanning-tree decomposition used in the final proof. The defect was located publicly in the problem’s discussion thread: on 25 March 2026 Tao observed that the invocation of Lemma 8 there is unjustified and that the flow lines need not organise into connected trees, and on 26 March 2026 the manuscript’s author agreed that the statement of Proposition 12 itself, not only its printed proof, is incorrect, and set the strategy aside. Section  records an independent diagnosis of the same local saddle defect, together with the Cassini obstruction to the printed global tree-length bound. That obstruction refutes the metric estimate used in the final proof, not Erdős #1041. Pendyala’s independent June 2026 preprint [11] proves the degree-four case through a finite four-point radial lemma and a short polygonal connector. That is the degree-four result directly comparable to the root-pair problem. Together with the cubic theorem established here, it settles these two degrees; it does not supply the general-degree conclusion. The all-degree estimates below either impose a bound on the least critical-value modulus or allow a larger length constant and containment level. They address different hypotheses from the quartic theorem.

What the formal links establish.

An ordinary mathematical argument is distinct from a proof checked by Lean. A linked declaration may prove a finite inequality without constructing the curve used here. Moreover, a declaration may be present in the versioned sources but absent from their recorded checked build. We distinguish these cases where the declarations are used. Neither a successful build nor an exact finite calculation establishes an unformalised analytic step.

Trinomials

Write Ef={z∈ℂ:|f(z)|<1}E_f=\{z\in\mathbb C:|f(z)|<1\}. The first theorem gives a prescribed path between every pair of zeros of a trinomial, in every degree.

Theorem 2.1 (trinomial root connections). Let n,mn,m be integers with 1≤m<n1\le m<n, and let f(z)=zn+azm+bf(z)=z^n+az^m+b have every zero in 𝔻\mathbb{D}. For every zero ζ\zeta, the segment [0,ζ][0,\zeta] lies in EfE_f. Consequently any two zeros ζ1,ζ2\zeta_1,\zeta_2 are joined in EfE_f by the broken line ζ1→0→ζ2\zeta_1\to0\to\zeta_2, of length |ζ1|+|ζ2|<2|\zeta_1|+|\zeta_2|<2.

Lean: all spokes, complete trinomial.

Proof. Vieta’s formula gives |b|<1|b|<1. At a zero ζ\zeta the root equation ζn+aζm+b=0\zeta^n+a\zeta^m+b=0 eliminates the middle coefficient: f(tζ)=b(1−tm)+ζn(tn−tm).\begin{equation} \label{eq:trinomial-cancellation} f(t\zeta)=b(1-t^m)+\zeta^n(t^n-t^m). \end{equation} For 0≤t<10\le t<1 the two scalar weights 1−tm1-t^m and tm−tnt^m-t^n are nonnegative and sum to 1−tn1-t^n, so |f(tζ)|≤|b|(1−tm)+|ζ|n(tm−tn)<1−tn≤1.|f(t\zeta)|\le|b|(1-t^m)+|\zeta|^n(t^m-t^n)<1-t^n\le1 . At t=1t=1 the value is zero. Concatenating two such segments gives the length assertion. ◻

The coefficient aa carries no hypothesis; the root equation removes it before absolute values are taken. The conclusion concerns segments to zeros and makes no assertion that EfE_f is star-shaped.

The cancellation mechanism.

For f(z)=∑k=0nckzkf(z)=\sum_{k=0}^nc_kz^k and a zero ζ\zeta, put Sj=∑k=0jckζkS_j=\sum_{k=0}^jc_k\zeta^k. Finite summation by parts gives f(tζ)=∑j=0n−1(tj−tj+1)Sj(0≤t≤1),\begin{equation} \label{eq:abel-control-polygon} f(t\zeta)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(t^j-t^{j+1})S_j\qquad(0\le t\le1), \end{equation} since the coefficient of ckζkc_k\zeta^k on the right is tk−tnt^k-t^n and ∑k<nckζk=−cnζn\sum_{k<n}c_k\zeta^k=-c_n\zeta^n. The weights in  are nonnegative and sum to 1−tn1-t^n, so the whole radial segment lies in the closed unit sublevel set whenever every partial sum lies in the closed unit disc. For a trinomial, Sj=bS_j=b for j<mj<m and Sj=−ζnS_j=-\zeta^n for m≤j<nm\le j<n; these two values may coincide. This is exactly the estimate above. With two intermediate coefficients, the root-disc hypothesis need not put every partial sum in the unit disc. The next example shows that a prescribed radial segment can then escape.

Example 2.2 (an escaping root spoke). Let 0<r<10<r<1 satisfy r6>320/327r^6>320/327, and set fr(z)=z6+15r2z4−15r4z2−r6=(z2−r2)(z4+65r2z2+r4).f_r(z)=z^6+\tfrac15r^2z^4-\tfrac15r^4z^2-r^6 =(z^2-r^2)\bigl(z^4+\tfrac65r^2z^2+r^4\bigr). Every zero has modulus rr: for the quartic factor put z=rwz=rw, so that the squared roots solve v2+(6/5)v+1=0v^2+(6/5)v+1=0, whose two roots are complex conjugates of product one. Nevertheless fr(r/2)=−327320r6,f_r(r/2)=-\frac{327}{320}\,r^6, so the segment [0,r][0,r] leaves EfrE_{f_r}. This rules out a universal assertion about every origin-to-zero segment. It exhibits no counterexample to the existence of some short connection.

Sources and scope.

The identity  is checked as the Abel summation identity, the constant-term bound as the constant-term estimate from the root-disc hypothesis, the radial estimate as containment along a trinomial root segment, and their combination with the length bound as the two segment inequalities and their length bound. Example  is checked as the sextic evaluation. What the kernel proves is the pair of radial inequalities and the bound |ζ1|+|ζ2|<2|\zeta_1|+|\zeta_2|<2 on the sum of the two radii. Assembling those into a single rectifiable path object, and the passage to the one-dimensional Hausdorff measure used by the original formulation of the problem, are ordinary steps taken here. No novelty claim is made for this elementary trinomial argument.

A small least critical value

The next criterion restricts the smallest critical-value modulus, but places no condition on the coefficients or the root locations. Throughout this section μ=minf′(c)=0|f(c)|\mu=\min_{f'(c)=0}|f(c)| is the least critical-value modulus.

Theorem 3.1 (a small least critical value forces a short connector). Let ff be squarefree and monic of degree n≥2n\ge2 with μ≤13/25\mu\le13/25. Then two distinct roots of ff are joined inside {|f|<1}\{|f|<1\} by a rectifiable curve of length strictly below 22. No hypothesis is placed on the locations of the roots, on the number of roots in any component, or on the capacity of any component.

Not formalised: the degree-two case and the exact rational arithmetic of the stopping-time comparison are checked, and the analytic argument in higher degrees is not. See the coverage section.

For f(z)=zn−bf(z)=z^n-b with 0<|b|<10<|b|<1, the only critical point is 00 and μ=|b|\mu=|b|. Thus this criterion includes |b|≤13/25|b|\le13/25 but excludes 13/25<|b|<113/25<|b|<1, although the trinomial theorem gives the required path in both ranges. Its value is that it also applies to polynomials with arbitrary coefficient patterns, including roots outside the unit disc. For example, (z−3)n−1/2(z-3)^n-1/2, n≥2n\ge2, has μ=1/2\mu=1/2 and all its roots satisfy |z|>2|z|>2. The required containment is |f(z)|<1|f(z)|<1, not |z|<1|z|<1.

Corollary 3.2 (scale-free form). Every squarefree monic ff of degree n≥2n\ge2 has two distinct roots joined inside {|f|<(25/13)μ}\{|f|<(25/13)\mu\} by a curve of length below 2((25/13)μ)1/n2\bigl((25/13)\mu\bigr)^{1/n}.

Lean: scaled low critical of low critical. Conditional on Theorem  as stated; see the coverage section.

Proof. Apply Theorem  to s−nf(sz)s^{-n}f(sz) with s=((25/13)μ)1/ns=\bigl((25/13)\mu\bigr)^{1/n}, whose least critical-value modulus is 13/2513/25, and scale back. Squarefreeness gives μ>0\mu>0, so the scaling factor is positive. ◻

The proof has two steps. Failure of the length bound first forces the roots to be far apart in the hyperbolic metric of a sublevel component. Packing those roots gives a lower bound for their number. Averaging paths between adjacent boundary points then converts that root count into an area-growth inequality. The rational certificate shows that this growth would exceed Pólya’s area bound before the value level reaches 11.

Consequences of having no short path.

Assume no two distinct roots are joined inside {|f|<1}\{|f|<1\} by a curve of length below 22. Choose a critical point at level μ\mu and two descending inverse arcs into distinct one-root components of {|f|<μ}\{|f|<\mu\}; below μ\mu each component maps conformally onto the value disc, and distinct local inverse arcs at the first critical point enter distinct components, since two inverse images of a nearby regular value in one component would contradict its degree one. Their union is a compact connected set containing two roots. Fix a level t∈(μ,1)t\in(\mu,1) at which no critical value has modulus tt, so that the level is regular. Let CtC_t be the component of {|f|<t}\{|f|<t\} containing that set, let k≥2k\ge2 be its root count, and put x=log⁡(t/μ)x=\log(t/\mu) and a=Area⁡(Ct)/πa=\operatorname{Area}(C_t)/\pi; Pólya’s inequality [2] gives a≤t2/n<1a\le t^{2/n}<1. The maximum principle, applied to that quotient and its reciprocal, makes it a unimodular constant. The product has degree kk, the root count of this component, not necessarily the full degree nn. There is also a point hh in the chosen compact connected set whose intrinsic distance in CtC_t from every root is at least 11. Otherwise the open intrinsic balls of radius 11 about the roots would cover that set. Two balls with distinct centres cannot meet: paths from their centres to a common point would concatenate to length below 22. But a connected set containing two distinct roots cannot be covered by these disjoint open sets. This contradiction proves the assertion. A lower bound for the number of roots.

Testing only consecutive pairs in angular order loses essential information. For k=2mk=2m, put mm points at hyperbolic radius dlowd_{\mathrm{low}} and mm at radius dlow+Dd_{\mathrm{low}}+D, alternating in cyclic order. The reverse triangle inequality separates every consecutive pair by at least DD, regardless of the angular gaps, whereas ∑jλ(dj)=m(λ(dlow)+λ(dlow+D))→∞(m→∞).\sum_j\lambda(d_j) =m\bigl(\lambda(d_{\mathrm{low}})+\lambda(d_{\mathrm{low}}+D)\bigr) \longrightarrow\infty\qquad(m\to\infty). The even number of points is needed for cyclic alternation. These point configurations test only the consecutive-pair constraints; they need not satisfy separation for nonconsecutive pairs or arise from a polynomial component. To use the missing pairwise information, we impose the packing bound on every circle centred at the origin.

The weighted sum of circle-slice inequalities is a dual certificate: it bounds the contribution of every permitted root configuration without having to optimise over all configurations directly. The weights give a usable bound only when Σ\Sigma and the supremum UU have rigorous bounds. In particular, checking the expression on a finite grid does not bound the supremum between grid points. Zero weights recover only the individual bound k≥2x/δ(a)k\ge2x/\delta(a); nonzero weights incorporate the circle-packing information and can improve the result. A certificate at area a′≥aa'\ge a also applies at aa. Indeed, dlow(a)≥dlow(a′)d_{\mathrm{low}}(a)\ge d_{\mathrm{low}}(a'), so the admissible range of dd only shrinks. Also D(a)≥D(a′)D(a)\ge D(a'), which enlarges every slice angle w(d,ri)w(d,r_i) at fixed d,rid,r_i. Since the weights are nonnegative, the expression defining UU can only decrease. Thus the same certified pair (Σ,U)(\Sigma,U) remains valid. The numerical comparison also uses two bounds that do not involve chosen weights. They are useful where the circle-slice certificate is weaker. We derive them here so that every root-count input to the comparison is visible.

Two further root-count bounds.

Order the distances as d1≤⋯≤dkd_1\le\cdots\le d_k. The triangle inequality gives dj≥D−d1d_j\ge D-d_1 for j≥2j\ge2. If d1≥D/2d_1\ge D/2, each summand is at most λ(D/2)\lambda(D/2) instead. (The definitions give dlow<D/2d_{\mathrm{low}}<D/2.) Thus x≤∑jλ(dj)≤max⁡{δ(a)2+(k−1)λ(D−dlow),kλ(D/2)},x\le\sum_j\lambda(d_j) \le\max\left\{ \frac{\delta(a)}2+(k-1)\lambda(D-d_{\mathrm{low}}),\; k\lambda(D/2)\right\}, and consequently k≥min⁡{1+x−δ(a)/2λ(D−dlow),xλ(D/2)}.k\ge\min\left\{ 1+\frac{x-\delta(a)/2}{\lambda(D-d_{\mathrm{low}})},\; \frac{x}{\lambda(D/2)}\right\}. The minimum is essential: the two expressions arise from alternative positions of the nearest root, not from simultaneous restrictions.

For the second bound, integrate over the disjoint hyperbolic balls of radius D/2D/2. Put E=e2/a−1E=e^{2/a}-1, so each ball has hyperbolic area 2πE2\pi E. At most one contains the origin; its contribution to ∑jλ(dj)\sum_j\lambda(d_j) is at most δ(a)/2\delta(a)/2. On every other ball, −log⁡|z|-\log|z| is harmonic. To average it, first move the ball’s centre to 00 by a disc automorphism. Hyperbolic area is invariant under this change of coordinates and has radial density 4/(1−|z|2)24/(1-|z|^2)^2 there. The ordinary mean-value property on each centred Euclidean circle therefore gives hyperbolic area mean λ(dj)\lambda(d_j). If the original ball has 00 on its boundary, use increasing smaller concentric balls and monotone convergence.

There are m=k−1m=k-1 nonexceptional balls if one contains the origin, and m=km=k otherwise. Their union has area 2πmE2\pi mE. Each superlevel set of −log⁡|z|-\log|z| is a centred ball, so its intersection with any set of this area has area at most the smaller of the two areas. The centred ball of area 2πmE2\pi mE attains that upper bound at every superlevel. Integrating these intersection areas over the superlevel parameter therefore bounds the integral over the union by the integral over that centred ball. Its radius RR satisfies cosh⁡R=1+mE\cosh R=1+mE. Sources and scope.

The analytic chain above is ordinary mathematics. Its general inputs are the Riemann mapping theorem, the Bergman kernel, the argument principle, the coarea formula, and Pólya’s area inequality Area⁡{|f|≤t}≤πt2/n\operatorname{Area}\{|f|\le t\}\le\pi t^{2/n} [1], . The exact rational certificate is checked by a separate exact-arithmetic program, not by the Lean kernel. The two additional root-count bounds above are the ordered-distance estimate in the earlier distance comparison and the area-rearrangement estimate in the hyperbolic packing argument. Their derivations above are part of the analytic proof. No complete Lean proof or independent review of this theorem is claimed. The finite summation implication identified in the companion paper assumes the geometric inequalities; it does not formalise the analytic chain or the certificate replay. Prior art for the assembled statement is unassessed. No novelty is claimed for the slice inequality, which follows directly from disjointness of the balls and the hyperbolic law of cosines. The public source of record is AngularBudgetLowCriticalClosure.md, which carries the full analytic argument, the table of certified weighted bounds and the instructions for replaying the certificate. The stopping-time test requires μ<e−X\mu<e^{-X}; the stated 13/2513/25 theorem and the 529/1000529/1000 consequence are two rational cutoffs within that range. Other theorems apply to some polynomials outside it, so failure of this numerical test does not identify the class left untreated by all the results. Fixed-degree arguments remain stronger at n=4n=4 and n=5n=5, where the corresponding thresholds are 61/10061/100 and 139/250139/250; from n=6n=6 on the all-degree constant 13/2513/25 is the better statement. These threshold arguments do not settle the unrestricted root-connector conclusion.

The next criterion uses logarithmic capacity, a measure of the size of a compact set that scales linearly under dilation. It compares the size of one component with that of the entire polynomial sublevel set. If that sublevel set is connected, the ratio κ\kappa below is 11; a cutoff such as κ≤1/3\kappa\le1/3 therefore requires a genuinely smaller component. The proof of Theorem  averages over levels in [μ,λμ][\mu,\lambda\mu]. To keep the path at the first critical level instead, one would need a perimeter estimate of the following kind. The regular-level argument (CF1) gives no finite pointwise bound at the critical level: even at a simple critical point, the area derivative diverges logarithmically.

The addendum [26] reports a Runge-approximation construction of monic level-one components with one simple zero and arbitrarily long analytic boundaries. It imposes neither a unit root disc nor a global lower bound on critical-value moduli. That proof was not supplied or available for checking in this revision; the report is not an input to the path estimates here. The question below requires a stronger hypothesis than the existence of one unramified component: the level must lie below every critical-value modulus of the polynomial. A construction without that global condition cannot by itself answer the question.

The preceding examples do not establish a universal perimeter bound. The implication below applies to an individual polynomial; a constant β\beta independent of the polynomial and degree would give a uniform path bound. The construction uses two components meeting at a first critical point and joins each root to that point at a cost of at most half its component’s perimeter. It does not give the constant 22 of the historical question.

Theorem 4.5 (a path from a subcritical perimeter bound). Let ff be squarefree and monic of degree n≥2n\ge2, and put μ=min⁡f′(c)=0|f(c)|>0\mu=\min_{f'(c)=0}|f(c)|>0. Then two distinct roots of ff are joined inside Kμ={|f|≤μ}K_\mu=\{|f|\le\mu\} by a rectifiable path of length at most βμ1/n\beta\mu^{1/n}.

Proof.

Put ρ=μ1/n\rho=\mu^{1/n}. On each component of {|f|<μ}\{|f|<\mu\}, ff is a proper unramified covering of the disc {|w|<μ}\{|w|<\mu\}, hence univalent. Equivalently, exhaust by regular levels below μ\mu and apply the component count [8]. At a critical point c*c_* with |f(c*)|=μ|f(c_*)|=\mu, the local degree d≥2d\ge2 gives dd nearby preimages of an inward radial value. Univalence places them in different one-root components. Choose two such components Ua,UbU_a,U_b, containing roots a,ba,b and with c*c_* in both closures; simplicity of c*c_* is unnecessary. For the boundary passage, take f(ϕ(w))=μwf(\phi(w))=\mu w on 𝔻\mathbb D. Fix |w0|=1|w_0|=1. The finitely many preimages of μw0\mu w_0 have disjoint neighbourhoods. Properness of ff and connectedness of a sufficiently small disc cap force ϕ\phi to stay in one of them as w→w0w\to w_0. At its preimage cc, write f(z)−f(c)=(z−c)dh(z),h(c)≠0.f(z)-f(c)=(z-c)^d h(z),\qquad h(c)\ne0. A local analytic ddth root of hh makes (z−c)h(z)1/d(z-c)h(z)^{1/d} a conformal coordinate. In each inverse sector, ϕ\phi is therefore an analytic function of (w−w0)1/d(w-w_0)^{1/d} and extends continuously to cc. The finitely many critical boundary values are the only exceptional points; at every other boundary value the ordinary inverse function theorem applies. Thus the extension is continuous on the closed disc and its boundary curve is rectifiable. The identity f(ϕ(eiθ))=μeiθf(\phi(e^{i\theta}))=\mu e^{i\theta} makes the boundary values injective, so the curve is Jordan.

As r↑1r\uparrow1, the curves ϕ(reiθ)\phi(re^{i\theta}) converge uniformly to that boundary and have length at most β(μr)1/n\beta(\mu r)^{1/n} by the hypothesis. Lower semicontinuity of length gives boundary length at most βρ\beta\rho for each component.

A bounded rectifiable Jordan domain UU has the following elementary property: any a∈Ua\in U can be joined to any c∈∂Uc\in\partial U in U¯\overline U with length at most ℋ1(∂U)/2\mathcal H^1(\partial U)/2. Of the two boundary arcs from uu to vv, write AA for the one containing cc and A′A' for the other. The paths from aa through uu or vv and then along AA to cc have total length |a−u|+|a−v|+length⁡(A)=|u−v|+length⁡(A)≤ℋ1(∂U),|a-u|+|a-v|+\operatorname{length}(A) =|u-v|+\operatorname{length}(A) \le\mathcal H^1(\partial U), because |u−v|≤length⁡(A′)|u-v|\le\operatorname{length}(A'). One path is at most half this sum. The connected interval ensures containment of the straight parts even when UU is not convex.

Apply this property in Ua,UbU_a,U_b with common boundary point c*c_*. Concatenating the two paths gives length at most 12(ℋ1(∂Ua)+ℋ1(∂Ub))≤βρ\tfrac12(\mathcal H^1(\partial U_a)+\mathcal H^1(\partial U_b)) \le\beta\rho, as required. Only these two component perimeters are used; the subcritical hypothesis bounds them by the limiting argument above. Boundary arcs are allowed, so containment is in KμK_\mu, not the open sublevel. ◻

Sources and scope.

Theorem  is ordinary mathematics. Its degenerate case μ=0\mu=0, its degree-two case and every numerical constant in its statement are checked in Lean; the analytic construction for degree at least three is used there as a hypothesis (Section ). The inputs of that construction are the capacity identity for polynomial preimages , Pólya’s area inequality [2], Cauchy–Schwarz, the Koebe distortion theorem for univalent maps, and averaging over adjacent boundary endpoints. The public source of record is the full area and boundary-length argument, which carries every rational verification quoted above. Its Section 10 gives a weaker conditional bound involving an auxiliary parameter and a logarithm; Theorem  states the stronger βρ\beta\rho consequence proved here. That section’s proposed numerical perimeter constant is refuted by the degree-eight example above and is not assumed in the theorem. The unconditional construction retains level 2μ2\mu and constant 71/1071/10. The scaled low-critical corollary has both a smaller constant and a smaller level. The proof retained here is ordinary, with component-sensitive consequences on their stated regions; its rational cutoffs are exact integer inequalities. The earlier perimeter samples concerned only a selected component. They do not test the stronger condition that the level lie below every critical value. The sharp root-connector conclusion is not established for the unrestricted class by the arguments in this record. The adjacent classical literature on lemniscate length concerns the arclength of the level curve {|p|=1}\{|p|=1\}, which is Erdős #114. Fryntov and Nazarov recall its history : Dolzhenko’s bound 4πn4\pi n, Pommerenke’s bound 74n274n^2 of 1961, and Borwein’s bound 8πen8\pi en [13]. Eremenko and Hayman proved 9.173n9.173n [14], Fryntov and Nazarov the asymptotically sharp 2n+o(n)2n+o(n) [15], and Tao resolved the problem for large nn [16]. These results bound the length of a level curve, not the least internal root-pair path. This distinction identifies the quantity being estimated; no claim of novelty follows from the scope or outcome of a literature search.

Degree three

A formal-source implementation includes the polygonal path, strict variation bound and repeated-root case; its recorded build status is stated below.

Sources and scope.

The source snapshot contains the complete degree-three path implementation and its supporting cubic source. This earlier implementation lies outside the main repository’s recorded checked build. The supplied release snapshot also contains the cubic theorem under monicity, degree three and the open-disc hypothesis and its expanded solution statement. The release proof obtains a root enumeration from monicity and degree; it does not assume an additional analytic path supplier. It constructs a continuous polygonal curve with bounded variation, values strictly below one and length strictly below two. Its endpoints are distinct when the polynomial is squarefree; repeated root occurrences are handled by the enumerated version. The supplied index classifies these release declarations as release_only, not ci_checked. The solution source contains a proof rather than the placeholder in the corresponding challenge file. This identifies the full formal target without claiming a fresh compilation or axiom audit. The proof above remains an ordinary mathematical argument. Pendyala [11] proves the separate quartic case; no historical priority for the cubic theorem is asserted here.

An all-degree critical-value separation theorem

The next theorem applies when one simple critical value is separated from all the others by a disc in the value plane. After a change of variables, the chosen critical point is 00 and its value is 11. The hypothesis below then says that the disc of centre w0w_0 and radius SS contains no other critical value. It is a condition to check, not an isolation property guaranteed for every polynomial.

The simplicity assumption means that the chosen critical point is a simple zero of the derivative, so two inverse branches meet there. A multiple chosen critical point is excluded; the other critical points need not be simple. Also, separation of roots in the zz-plane is not enough: different critical points can have nearly equal values. An exact quartic example below makes this distinction explicit. For a positive example, take f(z)=z3−3a2zf(z)=z^3-3a^2z with 0<a<1/30<a<1/\sqrt3. Its roots 0,±3a0,\pm\sqrt3a lie in the unit disc. At c=ac=a the critical value is v=−2a3v=-2a^3, and the other normalised critical value is −1-1. Thus the disc centred at 11 with radius 4/34/3 contains 00 and 11 but excludes the other critical value. Radius 22 is allowed as well: the other critical value then lies on the boundary. The proof must therefore allow a nonregular outer level.

Theorem 6.1 (separation of one simple critical value). Let PP be a polynomial of degree n≥3n\ge3 whose leading coefficient has modulus one, with P(0)=1,P′(0)=0,P″(0)≠0.P(0)=1,\qquad P'(0)=0,\qquad P''(0)\ne0. Sources and scope.

The two-sheeted component, its square-root uniformisation, the Bergman segment inequality, the component-capacity estimate, Pólya’s area–capacity inequality and the exhaustion are ordinary arguments. They are collected in the proof using an isolated critical value, whose capacity step is cited separately above. The separate Lean numerical kernel checks the coefficient bound for n≥3n\ge3, 4/3≤S≤24/3\le S\le2 and p≥0p\ge0, and the implication from the squared length bound to length below 22. It does not formalise the analytic hypotheses producing . The adjacent axiom-audit source names those numerical declarations; it is not an axiom audit of the ordinary analytic theorem.

The proof requires both a simple critical point and a disc centred on [0,1][0,1] that isolates its normalised value. For example, the trinomial zn−bz^n-b with n>2n>2 and 0<|b|<10<|b|<1 has a short path by Theorem , but its only critical point is not simple, so this method does not apply. The restriction is on the chosen critical point and on the distance of the other critical values from the chosen disc. The other critical points may be multiple, and their values need not be separated from one another. No sharpness is claimed for S=4/3S=4/3, and no assertion is made that every polynomial has a suitable isolated simple value. In particular, this is not a proof of the unrestricted assertion of Erdős #1041.

A related area comparison is Dubinin’s Theorem 1. The source is , Theorem 1 on printed page 85 of the POMI original. It concerns a holomorphic function that gives a full nn-fold covering of an annulus t1<|w|<t2t_1<|w|<t_2, and, in the notation of that theorem, with EE its explicitly defined complementary set, it states (t2t1)2/n≤m(E∪D)m(E).\Bigl(\frac{t_2}{t_1}\Bigr)^{2/n}\le\frac{m(E\cup D)}{m(E)}. The full covering and the explicit complementary set are hypotheses of the theorem. Tao cited it on the Erdős Problem #1041 discussion page on 25 March 2026 for the relative scaling factor s2/ns^{2/n} between the areas of two nested sublevel sets, which is the reading of the displayed inequality in which EE and E∪DE\cup D are those two sublevel sets and the covering hypothesis holds. No step of this note uses that relative inequality. The disk-family theorem instead uses Pólya’s absolute area–capacity inequality on a component containing fewer than nn roots, after the component-capacity estimate supplies its strict capacity gap. The absolute sublevel inequality Area⁡{|P|<T}≤πT2/n\operatorname{Area}\{|P|<T\}\le\pi T^{2/n} remains the area input to Theorem  and to Theorem . Dubinin’s theorem is a neighbouring result under a full covering hypothesis and supplies no root connector.

Collinear roots and two sparse polynomial families

The following results impose concrete restrictions: roots on one line, a quintic with two missing coefficients, or a polynomial of the form P((z−h)q)P((z-h)^q) with PP cubic. None covers a general polynomial with roots in the unit disc. We first state the finite inequalities used in their proofs, then explain how the inequalities produce contained paths. The formal links distinguish these two steps.

Collinear roots and Chebyshev comparison

The extreme zeros of TnT_n are ±cos⁡(π/(2n))\pm\cos(\pi/(2n)). Scaling them to ±1\pm1 makes the comparison polynomial have the same endpoint zeros as the polynomial under study; dividing by its leading coefficient makes both polynomials monic. Their difference then has smaller degree. Accordingly, put rn=cos⁡π2n,Cn=12n−1rnn.r_n=\cos\frac{\pi}{2n}, \qquad C_n=\frac{1}{2^{n-1}r_n^n}.

Theorem 7.1 (Chebyshev comparison). Let m≥0m\ge0, let p∈ℝ[X]p\in\mathbb R[X] be monic of degree m+2m+2, and let −1<c0<⋯<cm<1,|ci|≤1.-1<c_0<\cdots<c_m<1,\qquad |c_i|\le1. Suppose p(−1)=p(1)=0p(-1)=p(1)=0 and p(ci)p(ci+1)<0p(c_i)p(c_{i+1})<0 for 0≤i<m0\le i<m. Then min0≤i≤m|p(ci)|≤Cm+2.\min_{0\le i\le m}|p(c_i)|\le C_{m+2}.

This is exactly the statement selected as the formal Chebyshev endpoint. It proves the finite alternation inequality; it does not yet construct the segment between two roots.

All real-rooted polynomials, and their images under rotations and translations, satisfy the collinearity hypothesis. Three noncollinear roots already fall outside it. The gain is an explicit sharp bound for the modulus along one adjacent-root segment, not a bound obtained by assuming that segment is contained.

Theorem 7.2 (a sharp bound for collinear roots). Let ff be a monic polynomial of degree n≥2n\ge2 whose zero occurrences are collinear, and let DD be their diameter. Some two adjacent zero occurrences are joined by a segment of length at most DD on which |f(z)|≤(D/2)n2n−1cos⁡n(π/(2n)).|f(z)|\le \frac{(D/2)^n}{2^{n-1}\cos^n(\pi/(2n))}. \tag{9} The constant in (9) is best possible in every degree. Equality is attained by affine images of the zeros of TnT_n whose extreme zeros have distance DD.

Critical sequences and the extremal configuration.

For distinct real zeros, each gap between consecutive zeros contains exactly one zero of q′q', and |q||q| attains its maximum over the gap only there. The points cic_i chosen in the proof of Theorem  are therefore the critical points of qq, and the gap maxima are the moduli of its ordered critical sequence (q(c1),…,q(cn−1))(q(c_1),\ldots,q(c_{n-1})), with c1<⋯<cn−1c_1<\cdots<c_{n-1}. In this distinct-root setting, the ordered sequence determines the real polynomial up to an increasing real affine change of variable . The proof above uses only the alternation count, not this classification theorem. In this language, (9) says that a real polynomial of degree nn with nn distinct real zeros, leading coefficient aa and zero diameter DD has a critical value of modulus at most Cn|a|(D/2)nC_n|a|(D/2)^n.

The comparison polynomial q*q_* is the monic polynomial of least deviation from zero on [−1/rn,1/rn][-1/r_n,1/r_n], characterised by the equioscillation conditions recalled in . All n−1n-1 of its critical values have modulus CnC_n, so every critical point of q*q_* lies on the level curve {|q*|=Cn}\{|q_*|=C_n\}. Extremals with this property also occur in the level-curve length problem, where some extremal polynomial has all its critical points on {|p|=1}\{|p|=1\} [14], and in the sharp bound for |f′||f'| on a connected sublevel set {|f|≤1}\{|f|\le1\} of a monic polynomial, proved by Eremenko and Lempert , whose equality cases are e−inθTn(21/n−1eiθz+b)e^{-in\theta}T_n(2^{1/n-1}e^{i\theta}z+b) with θ\theta real [19].

Formal scope.

Lean checks sign preservation, the alternating root-count mechanism, the scaled Chebyshev endpoint and uniform bound, and Theorem . It does not check the rigid normalization, the existence of the gap maxima, transport back to the root line, or the equality-node locations used in Theorem . These are ordinary steps. The sharpness assertion concerns the maximum of |f||f| on the selected adjacent-root segment, and the displayed configurations attain it; no claim is made that they exhaust the equality cases, and no claim is made that the selected segment is a shortest path in {|f|<1}\{|f|<1\}.

Formal scope.

The moment identities and the inequality selecting two indices have formal proofs. The source snapshot additionally contains a complete implementation of the open-disc sparse-quintic path conclusion, including the geometric assembly. The formal-source index places the complete open-disc path conclusion in its checked build. That declaration does not by itself assert every closed-disc equality clause of the longer theorem above. That is supplied build evidence, not a new compilation performed for this prose revision. The ordinary argument above is retained, and the source link remains at its original commit.

Polynomials obtained from a cubic by a power substitution

For f(z)=P((z−h)q)f(z)=P((z-h)^q), the roots associated with a nonzero root of PP form a regular qq-gon centred at hh. This rotational symmetry is a substantial restriction: a generic polynomial of degree 3q3q does not have it. It lets one contained segment for the cubic give two segments in the original variable. The first theorem supplies that segment.

Formal scope.

Lean checks the identity for these three real numbers, the choice of a contained cubic segment, and the quartic counterexample, and also the complete translated cubic fibre theorem. The latter supplies the finite set of roots in each fibre, root-of-unity average, nonzero-root selection, pullback and explicit rectifiable path through the centre under the hypotheses displayed above. Its exact source occurs in the successfully compiled dependency closure of the source-bound Lean build and axiom-audit record. The theorem gives length below 22; the sharper 21−|h|22\sqrt{1-|h|^2} reading in the proof is recorded here as an ordinary consequence of the mean-square identity, not as a separately audited endpoint.

Scope of the formal results.

The finite declarations prove the Chebyshev comparison, the two-index quintic inequality and the cubic segment estimate. The formal-source index also records complete path theorems for the sparse quintic and the translated cubic family in its checked build. These are stronger than the finite inequalities alone. The sharper bound 21−|h|22\sqrt{1-|h|^2} and the quartic lifting arguments below retain the ordinary proof status stated beside them. A formal declaration must still be compared with the exact hypotheses and conclusion of the paper statement; a similar name is not enough.

Further families and counterexamples to proposed proof steps

The following sections collect additional sufficient conditions and counterexamples to particular path constructions. They are not a programme for proving the unrestricted historical assertion. The underlying research notes are retained at commit f214a6b4 and summarised in the dated overview of these arguments. Where a claim is based on a computation rather than a proof, that restriction is stated explicitly.

Equality holds at the midpoint, where θ=0\theta=0. Consequently the maximum on every such chord is exactly rn+(sc)nr^n+(sc)^n. Taking s=rs=r proves the outer threshold; taking s=t=ε/c≤rs=t=\varepsilon/c\le r proves the inner bound, and taking s=λt<ts=\lambda t<t makes it strict. Every radial leg between ss and rr has modulus rn−|z|n<1r^n-|z|^n<1. Its two legs and crossing chord have length 2r−2s(1−sin⁡(π/n))<2r2r-2s(1-\sin(\pi/n))<2r, which proves the stated length formula and shows that contraction preserves the strict length bound.

For n=2n=2, the chord is a diameter and its maximum is r2<1r^2<1; its length is 2r<22r<2. For n≥3n\ge3, the outer chord works exactly when r<r*r<r_*, and its length is 2rsin⁡(π/n)2r\sin(\pi/n). At r=r*r=r_* it reaches level one at its midpoint. If r≥r*r\ge r_*, the two radial legs and inner crossing have length 2r−2εtan⁡(π4−π2n)<2r<2.2r-2\varepsilon\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\frac\pi{2n}\right)<2r<2. Contracting the crossing radius makes the level bound strict, as proved above. The argument compares these constructions, not their lengths with all admissible paths.

A bounded-radius concyclic class

A different argument gives a chord when all roots lie on a circle of sufficiently small radius. Let ff be monic of degree n≥3n\ge3 with distinct zeros on a circle of radius ρ\rho. If 2ρn≤12\rho^n\le1, two adjacent zeros are joined by their straight chord, whose length is at most 2ρsin⁡(π/n)<22\rho\sin(\pi/n)<2, and the chord lies in {|f|<1}\{|f|<1\}. (If a zero is repeated, the short-connection conclusion is immediate; the distinct case is the substantive one.)

For each fixed degree nn, the radius condition is ρ≤2−1/n\rho\le2^{-1/n}. It allows arbitrary spacing on that circle, but does not cover every radius ρ<1\rho<1. No restriction on the circle’s centre is imposed.

After translating and scaling, let gg be the monic polynomial with roots w1,…,wnw_1,\ldots,w_n on the unit circle. Such a polynomial is self-inversive: zng(1/z¯)¯z^n\overline{g(1/\overline z)} is a constant multiple of g(z)g(z), with the constant of modulus one. Equivalently, e−inθ/2g(eiθ)e^{-in\theta/2}g(e^{i\theta}) is real up to a fixed phase. Choose c=(−1)n+1∏jwj,q(z)=zn−c.c=(-1)^{n+1}\prod_j w_j,\qquad q(z)=z^n-c. Then gg and qq have the same leading and constant coefficients, and their boundary values have a common real phase. If every root gap contained a point with |g|>|q||g|>|q|, the real boundary function of g−qg-q would have alternating signs at these points. Advancing the angle by 2π2\pi multiplies that function by (−1)n(-1)^n, so the alternation also holds across the final gap. The intermediate value theorem would give nn distinct unit-circle zeros of g−qg-q. This is impossible: its degree is at most n−1n-1, and g=qg=q cannot satisfy the assumed strict inequalities. Thus some adjacent-root arc satisfies |g|≤|q|≤2|g|\le|q|\le2. The interior of that arc contains no zero of qq, since gg is nonzero there. As consecutive zeros of qq are separated by angle 2π/n2\pi/n, the selected arc has angular width at most 2π/n2\pi/n. This explains why the same selected pair also has the required short chord. To pass from this arc to its chord [a,b][a,b], let ν\nu be the unit normal pointing into the circular segment bounded by them. On the open chord, logarithmic differentiation gives ∂νlog⁡|g(z)|=∑wj∉{a,b}Re⁡(νz−wj¯)|z−wj|2>0.\partial_\nu\log|g(z)| =\sum_{w_j\notin\{a,b\}} \frac{\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\nu\overline{z-w_j}\bigr)}{|z-w_j|^2}>0. The endpoint terms vanish because their directions are tangent to the chord. Every remaining numerator is positive because the other roots lie strictly on the far side of its line; n≥3n\ge3 ensures at least one such term. The harmonic function log⁡|g|\log|g| has no interior maximum and tends to −∞-\infty at a,ba,b. A maximum cannot lie on the open chord either, since moving into the circular segment increases the function. It is therefore attained on the arc, and the maximum on the chord is strictly smaller. Scaling back gives |f|<2ρn≤1|f|<2\rho^n\le1 throughout the chord, with f=0f=0 at its endpoints. These are the arguments of Theorem C and Lemma S, Sections 3–4 of the concyclic note.

The argument is an ordinary proof outside Lean. The exact-rational checker checks finitely many identities used in the proof and configurations, while the numerical checker is regression and stress-test evidence. The arc constant 22 is attained by the regular nn-gon. Thus the bound obtained by passing through the arc is ρ≤2−1/n\rho\le2^{-1/n}, although this cutoff tends to 11 as n→∞n\to\infty. This does not assert optimality of the chord bound or exclude another contained path at a larger radius. Nor does arc sharpness make the pair of radial segments shortest. For example, for g(z)=z3−1/8g(z)=z^3-1/8 the chord between 1/21/2 and e2πi/3/2e^{2\pi i/3}/2 has length 3/2<1\sqrt3/2<1, whereas the two radii have total length 11. The binomial calculation above gives a maximum of 9/64<19/64<1 on that chord. The length-22 equality at zn−1z^n-1, proved below, concerns the uncontracted closed-level problem.

Power substitutions in trinomials

The radial-segment identity and strict bound are formalized in cancellation along a trinomial root segment and containment of a trinomial root segment.

The trinomial identity also applies after a power substitution. Fix integers 1≤r<m1\le r<m and q≥1q\ge1, and consider the translated monic polynomial f(z)=(z−h)qm+a(z−h)qr+c.f(z)=(z-h)^{qm}+a(z-h)^{qr}+c. The strict exponent inequality keeps the leading monomial separate. The algebraic identity below also holds when r=mr=m, but then the two leading terms merge and the displayed polynomial need not be monic or have degree qmqm. Writing w=(z−h)qw=(z-h)^q reduces the root equation to wm+awr+c=0w^m+aw^r+c=0. At such a quotient root the middle coefficient can be eliminated exactly: for 0≤u≤10\le u\le1, umwm+aurwr+c=(1−ur)c−(ur−um)wm.u^mw^m+au^rw^r+c =(1-u^r)c-(u^r-u^m)w^m. This is a nonnegative combination of cc and −wm-w^m, with weights 1−ur1-u^r and ur−umu^r-u^m summing to 1−um1-u^m. The formal radial-segment estimate gives strict containment when |w|<1|w|<1 and |c|<1|c|<1.

For q≥2q\ge2 and a nonzero quotient root satisfying these bounds, choose two distinct solutions y1,y2y_1,y_2 of yq=wy^q=w. Their common modulus is |w|1/q<1|w|^{1/q}<1. To lift a quotient radial segment, set u=tqu=t^q: |f(h+tyi)|≤(1−tqm)max⁡{|c|,|w|m}<1(0≤t≤1).|f(h+ty_i)| \le (1-t^{qm})\max\{|c|,|w|^m\}<1 \qquad(0\le t\le1). Thus the two lifted segments join h+y1h+y_1 to h+y2h+y_2 through hh with length 2|w|1/q<22|w|^{1/q}<2. The construction uses any quotient root with the stated modulus bound; it does not prove that such a root exists without an additional hypothesis. A zero quotient root instead gives a root of multiplicity at least qq at hh and hence a constant path between two occurrences. The formal source checks the factorization, radial-segment estimate and finite length inequality. It does not establish the existence of a suitable quotient root or formalise the selection and lifting just described. Thus its scope is the segment inequality and finite length calculation, not the complete path construction or unrestricted Erdős #1041.

A coefficient condition for four-term polynomials

With one additional monomial, Abel summation gives a sufficient condition involving the two lower coefficients. Let g(w)=wm+awr+bws+c,m>r>s≥1,g(w)=w^m+aw^r+bw^s+c,\qquad m>r>s\ge1, assume all roots of gg lie in the open unit disk, and let w1,w2w_1,w_2 be roots of the two smallest moduli. If |c|+|b||w2|s<1,|c|+|b|\,|w_2|^s<1, then the complete radial spokes from w1w_1 and w2w_2 to the origin lie in {|g|<1}\{|g|<1\}, and their broken line has length strictly below 22. The simpler coefficient condition |b|+|c|≤1|b|+|c|\le1 makes every root-to-origin segment contained; the coefficient aa has no additional restriction beyond the assumed root locations. This coefficient condition includes b=0b=0 and |c|≤1|c|\le1, but is not automatic for all four-term polynomials with roots in the disc.

The mechanism is visible in one identity. At a root ww and for 0≤u≤10\le u\le1, g(uw)=(1−us)c+(us−ur)(c+bws)+(ur−um)(−wm).\begin{split} g(uw)={}&(1-u^s)c +(u^s-u^r)(c+bw^s) +(u^r-u^m)(-w^m). \end{split} Here the root equation has eliminated awraw^r before taking absolute values. The three weights are nonnegative and sum to 1−um1-u^m. The controlled terms are cc, c+bwsc+bw^s and −wm-w^m; their moduli are strictly below one under the root-dependent condition. The same identity explains why no bound on aa is needed. Lean checks the factorization and the resulting strict spoke theorem under the exact weak exponent hypotheses 1≤s≤r≤m1\le s\le r\le m; it also checks the coefficient-only corollary above. Its weak bound |b|+|c|≤1|b|+|c|\le1 still gives strict containment: the root-disc hypothesis implies |c|<1|c|<1, and, if b≠0b\ne0, |w|s<1|w|^s<1 gives |c|+|b||w|s<|c|+|b|≤1|c|+|b||w|^s<|c|+|b|\le1. If b=0b=0, the required bound is simply |c|<1|c|<1.

An alternative criterion uses a complex power sum to select two indices. Let SS index a finite family of roots, N=|S|≥2N=|S|\ge2, and M=∑i∈Swis.M=\sum_{i\in S}w_i^s. The squared-modulus identity gives ∑i∈S|c+bwis|2=N|c|2+|b|2∑i∈S|wis|2+2Re⁡(c¯bM).\sum_{i\in S}|c+bw_i^s|^2 =N|c|^2+|b|^2\sum_{i\in S}|w_i^s|^2 +2\mathop\mathrm{Re}(\overline c\,bM). Consequently, if every |wi|<1|w_i|<1, |c|<1|c|<1, and N(|b|2+|c|2)+2Re⁡(c¯bM)<N−1,N\bigl(|b|^2+|c|^2\bigr) +2\mathop\mathrm{Re}(\overline c\,bM)<N-1, then two distinct indices i,j∈Si,j\in S satisfy |c+bwis|<1|c+bw_i^s|<1 and |c+bwjs|<1|c+bw_j^s|<1. Indeed, the displayed identity bounds the sum of squared moduli strictly below N−1N-1. If at most one index had modulus below one, the other N−1N-1 terms would each contribute at least one. This explains both the threshold N−1N-1 and why the criterion selects two indices. Applying the resulting contained-segment theorem to these inequalities proves that both root segments lie strictly in {|g|<1}\{|g|<1\}. Retaining the signed cross term permits the inequality to hold for configurations outside the coefficient-only triangle |b|+|c|≤1|b|+|c|\le1. The formal hypotheses do not require i↦wii\mapsto w_i to be injective, so distinct indices need not denote distinct root values. For the polynomial consequence, the family must be a submultiset of the zeros, respecting their algebraic multiplicities. A repeated zero then already gives a constant path between two occurrences. Repeating a simple zero in an arbitrary indexed family cannot supply a second occurrence. The two sufficient conditions are not ordered by strength. For example, g(w)=w5+19/20g(w)=w^5+19/20 has all roots in the open unit disc and satisfies the coefficient condition with b=0b=0. For its full five-root list, however, the left side of the power-sum condition is 5(19/20)2=361/80>4=N−15(19/20)^2=361/80>4=N-1, so that condition fails. Its benefit is the use of cancellation in the cross term, not inclusion of every case covered by the coefficient condition. Conversely, g(w)=(w2−1/2)(w3+4/5)=w5−12w3+45w2−25g(w)=(w^2-1/2)(w^3+4/5) =w^5-\tfrac12w^3+\tfrac45w^2-\tfrac25 has all roots of modulus 1/21/\sqrt2 or (4/5)1/3(4/5)^{1/3}, hence below one, but |b|+|c|=6/5>1|b|+|c|=6/5>1. Its full root list has M=∑iwi2=1M=\sum_iw_i^2=1: the two quadratic roots contribute 11, and the three cubic roots contribute 00. The power-sum left side is 5(16/25+4/25)−16/25=84/25<45(16/25+4/25)-16/25=84/25<4. Thus this criterion does cover root-disc polynomials excluded by the coefficient condition.

For q≥2q\ge2 and f(z)=g((z−h)q)f(z)=g((z-h)^q), assume also that all roots of ff lie in the open unit disc. If yq=wy^q=w and ω=e2πi/q\omega=e^{2\pi i/q}, the roots h+ωjyh+\omega^j y satisfy 1q∑j=0q−1|h+ωjy|2=|h|2+|y|2<1.\frac1q\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}|h+\omega^j y|^2=|h|^2+|y|^2<1. Thus every quotient root has |w|=|y|q<1|w|=|y|^q<1, which supplies the root-disc hypothesis used above, and every lifted spoke has length |y|<1|y|<1. Two selected spokes join through hh with total length below 22; repeated root occurrences instead permit the constant path. The Lean theorem assumes the finite root family, its complex power sum MM, and the displayed inequality. It neither derives that inequality from arbitrary coefficients nor verifies the family’s polynomial multiplicities, the cyclic lifting, or the final path construction. Completeness of the root list is not required for the selection argument: a submultiset respecting multiplicity suffices. Without one of the power-sum, root-dependent, or coefficient-only inequalities, the tetranomial case is not covered by this argument; this family does not solve unrestricted Erdős #1041.

A quartic composed with a power map

Pendyala’s degree-four theorem [11], with his four-point radial lemma , can also be lifted through every nontrivial cyclic power. Let PP be a monic quartic, let q≥2q\ge2 be an integer, and set f(z)=P((z−h)q).f(z)=P((z-h)^q). Assume that every root of ff lies in the open unit disc. A repeated root of ff gives the constant path, so suppose ff is squarefree. Then the roots of PP are distinct and nonzero. For a root w=yqw=y^q of PP, all points h+ζjyh+\zeta^j y, with ζ=e2πi/q\zeta=e^{2\pi i/q}, are roots of ff. Hence the open-disc hypothesis gives 1q∑j=0q−1|h+ζjy|2=|h|2+|y|2<1.\frac1q\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}|h+\zeta^jy|^2=|h|^2+|y|^2<1. In particular |w|1/q=|y|<1|w|^{1/q}=|y|<1, which is the bound needed for the lifted length, and also |w|<1|w|<1. Pendyala’s chord-or-radial argument supplies the quotient geometry in two cases. If two quotient roots satisfy |wi−wj|<1|w_i-w_j|<1, every point ww of the chord [wi,wj][w_i,w_j] lies in the unit disc; the two endpoint factors of |P(w)||P(w)| have product at most |wi−wj|2/4|w_i-w_j|^2/4 and the other two factors are below 22, so |P(w)|≤|wi−wj|2<1|P(w)|\le|w_i-w_j|^2<1. Otherwise the quotient roots are pairwise at distance at least 11. Choosing RR with max⁡k|wk|<R<1\max_k|w_k|<R<1 and applying the four-point radial lemma to the points wk/Rw_k/R gives distinct i,ji,j with |P(twi)|≤R4|P(tw_i)|\le R^4 and |P(twj)|≤R4|P(tw_j)|\le R^4 for 0≤t≤10\le t\le1, so the radial segments [0,wi][0,w_i] and [0,wj][0,w_j] lie in {|P|<1}\{|P|<1\}. The extra issue is metric: a short chord in the ww-plane need not lift isometrically through y↦yqy\mapsto y^q.

Put α=1/q\alpha=1/q. On a chord avoiding 00, choose a continuous argument and hence a root lift yy with yq=wy^q=w. Differentiation gives |dy|=α|w|α−1|dw||dy|=\alpha|w|^{\alpha-1}|dw|, independently of the chosen root. If the supporting line has distance dd from 00, and xx is distance along that line from the perpendicular foot, then (d2+x2)α−1≤xα−1(x>0).\bigl(\sqrt{d^2+x^2}\bigr)^{\alpha-1} \le x^{\alpha-1}\qquad(x>0). The negative exponent is why replacing |w||w| by xx gives an upper length bound. Lean checks the integral of the power-map derivative α∫0Axα−1dx=Aα.\alpha\int_0^A x^{\alpha-1}\,dx=A^\alpha. If the foot lies on the chord, split there: the two integrals are bounded by the α\alpha-powers of the distances from the foot to the endpoints, hence by |a|α+|b|α|a|^\alpha+|b|^\alpha. If the foot lies outside the chord, integrate on one side of it; extending the interval to the foot bounds the result by the α\alpha-power of the farther endpoint’s modulus. When the chord passes through 00, choose a continuous root on each half and join the lifts at 00; the integral is finite because α>0\alpha>0. This proves the chord-lift estimate length⁡([a,b]̃)≤|a|1/q+|b|1/q.\operatorname{length}(\widetilde{[a,b]}) \le |a|^{1/q}+|b|^{1/q}. The strict endpoint-length estimate also proves that if 0≤a,b<10\le a,b<1, α>0\alpha>0, and a candidate length LL is at most aα+bαa^\alpha+b^\alpha, then L<2L<2. The close-pair chord therefore has a lift of length below 22. In the other case the quotient arms meet at 00, so their lifts are radial segments meeting at hh, with total length |wi|1/q+|wj|1/q<2|w_i|^{1/q}+|w_j|^{1/q}<2. In both cases f=P∘((z−h)q)f=P\circ((z-h)^q) transfers containment from the quotient curve. Distinct quotient endpoints give distinct roots of ff. This proves the path assertion in every degree 4q≥84q\ge8. The fibre average gives a little more: |h|<1|h|<1 and |wk|1/q<1−|h|2|w_k|^{1/q}<\sqrt{1-|h|^2} for every quotient root. Consequently the same constructed path has length length⁡<21−|h|2≤2.\operatorname{length}<2\sqrt{1-|h|^2}\le2. This refinement concerns the translated power-substitution family, not arbitrary degree-4q4q polynomials.

Pendyala proves the quartic geometric theorem and its four-point radial lemma. The local Lean module checks the antitone density inequality, its integral, the strict powered endpoint-length bound, and the final length estimate. It does not formalize Pendyala’s geometric lemma, the continuous covering-space construction of the root lift, or the ordinary chord/radial case assembly. This is a family defined by a power substitution, not a proof of unrestricted Erdős #1041.

The joining point in the quartic construction.

Pendyala’s proof of [11] uses a smallest enclosing disc and joins the selected roots through its centre. For the power substitution we instead apply [11] to the centred disc |w|≤R|w|\le R. That lemma requires only the disc and pairwise-distance hypotheses, not minimality of the disc. Keeping the joining point at 00 is what makes the radial lift above valid. The endpoint-length bound for a single chord would not justify lifting an arbitrary broken line through a nonzero quotient vertex.

A mean bound for critical values in every degree

The next theorem gives the quadratic case of a Poisson argument for critical-value moments. It allows a disc of any centre and radius, repeated roots, and repeated critical points. After proving this case, we derive the stronger exponent 4/(n−1)4/(n-1) and explain how vanishing complex power sums permit still larger exponents. None of these moment bounds controls the lengths of inverse paths ending at the critical points.

Dubinin [21] proves the sharp unit-disc critical-value product inequality using the resultant identity, the maximum-modulus principle and Schur’s Vandermonde inequality. The positive-moment estimate below implies his product bound by AM–GM. When n≥3n\ge3, the product estimate alone cannot control a positive moment: a list T,T−1,1,…,1T,T^{-1},1,\ldots,1 has product one, but its sum of ppth powers is unbounded as T→∞T\to\infty for every p>0p>0. This compares the information in two inequalities for nonnegative lists; it does not claim that these lists occur as critical values of polynomials in the theorem. In degree two there is just one critical value, and the product and positive-moment bounds are equivalent. For a zero prescribed at the origin, his Theorem 3 (p. 1174) gives (∏j|f(cj)|)1/(n−1)≤(n−1)(|f′(0)|2nn)1/(n−1).\left(\prod_j|f(c_j)|\right)^{1/(n-1)} \le(n-1)\left(\frac{|f'(0)|^2}{n^n}\right)^{1/(n-1)}. Dubinin explicitly identifies Tischler’s earlier contribution . His Theorem 1 uses dissymmetrisation; that is not the proof mechanism of Theorem 2. Schur’s original paper [27] is the historical antecedent cited there, not a separately re-proved source in this record. A sharp marked-zero positive-moment bound remains a separate question. The addendum [26] reports a reduction to boundary-root configurations, without solving the resulting angular optimisation. That unavailable addendum is not a proof dependency of the critical-value theorem below.

Theorem 8.1 (a mean bound for critical values). Let ff be monic of degree n≥2n\ge2, with roots in a closed disc of radius R≥0R\ge0. If c1,…,cn−1c_1,\ldots,c_{n-1} are its critical points counted with multiplicity, then ∑j=1n−1|f(cj)|2/(n−1)≤(n−1)R2n/(n−1).\begin{equation} \label{eq:critical-value-quadratic-budget} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1}|f(c_j)|^{2/(n-1)} \le(n-1)R^{2n/(n-1)}. \end{equation} Consequently the lower exponents used elsewhere in the record satisfy ∑j=1n−1|f(cj)|1/(n−1)≤(n−1)Rn/(n−1)\begin{equation} \label{eq:critical-value-power-budget} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1}|f(c_j)|^{1/(n-1)} \le(n-1)R^{n/(n-1)} \end{equation} and ∑j=1n−1|f(cj)|1/n≤(n−1)R.\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}|f(c_j)|^{1/n}\le(n-1)R. The constant is attained by f(z)=(z−τ)n−λf(z)=(z-\tau)^n-\lambda with enclosing disk centred at τ\tau and radius R=|λ|1/nR=|\lambda|^{1/n}.

Lean: critical value three budgets, critical value three budgets sharp.

The finite inequality behind the theorem concerns arbitrary points of the disk, without asking them to arise as critical points. Its quadratic form is ∑j=1m(∏k=1m|1−cj¯ck|)2/m≤m,|cj|≤1.\sum_{j=1}^m\left(\prod_{k=1}^m |1-\overline{c_j}c_k|\right)^{2/m}\le m, \qquad |c_j|\le1. The following pointwise bound explains why these finite inequalities control critical values in every degree.

Lemma 8.2 (reflected-derivative bound). If ff is monic of degree n≥2n\ge2 with roots in the closed unit disk, and c1,…,cn−1c_1,\ldots,c_{n-1} list its critical points with multiplicity, then |f(cj)|≤∏k=1n−1|1−cj¯ck|.\begin{equation} \label{eq:critical-reflected-product} |f(c_j)|\le\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}|1-\overline{c_j}c_k|. \end{equation}

Lean: reflected critical value.

The reflected-derivative inequality is checked in Lean, including closed-disc roots and critical-point multiplicities.

Proof. First put all roots aia_i strictly inside the disk. We want a numerator that equals nfnf at the critical points and can be compared with f′f' on the circle. Set N(z)=nf(z)−zf′(z),G(z)=n∏k(1−ck¯z).N(z)=nf(z)-zf'(z),\qquad G(z)=n\prod_k(1-\overline{c_k}z). The numerator is the polar derivative at 00: the conventional polar derivative at α\alpha is nf(z)+(α−z)f′(z)nf(z)+(\alpha-z)f'(z); see Rather–Gulzar, Section 1 for this notation. Its leading term cancels, and N(cj)=nf(cj)N(c_j)=nf(c_j). Reflection gives |G|=|f′||G|=|f'| on the circle. Gauss–Lucas puts every ckc_k inside the disc, so GG has no zero on its closure. Thus N/GN/G is a holomorphic quotient to which the maximum-modulus principle applies. On |ζ|=1|\zeta|=1, Re⁡ζf′(ζ)f(ζ)=∑i(12+1−|ai|22|1−aiζ‾|2)≥n2.\operatorname{Re}\frac{\zeta f'(\zeta)}{f(\zeta)} =\sum_i\left(\frac12+ \frac{1-|a_i|^2}{2|1-a_i\bar\zeta|^2}\right)\ge\frac n2. Writing the logarithmic derivative as ww, the identity |n−w|2−|w|2=n2−2nRe⁡w≤0|n-w|^2-|w|^2=n^2-2n\operatorname{Re}w\le0 gives |N|≤|G||N|\le|G| on the circle. The maximum-modulus principle applied to N/GN/G gives the same comparison inside. At cjc_j, N(cj)=nf(cj)N(c_j)=nf(c_j); dividing by nn and conjugating each factor proves . For closed-disk roots apply this result to fr(z)=rnf(z/r)f_r(z)=r^nf(z/r), 0<r<10<r<1, whose critical points are rckrc_k: rn|f(cj)|≤∏k|1−r2cj¯ck|.r^n|f(c_j)|\le\prod_k|1-r^2\overline{c_j}c_k|. Area of a connected sublevel set.

Limits of contained paths at fixed degree

The compactness argument used in Section 17 of the short note is given here in full. It concerns arbitrary contained curves, not a prescribed pair of inverse rays.

Fix n≥2n\ge2, and let 𝒦n\mathcal K_n be the compact coefficient class of monic degree-nn polynomials with roots in the closed unit disc. Define Λ(f)=infγlength⁡(γ),\Lambda(f)=\inf_\gamma\operatorname{length}(\gamma), where γ⊂{|f|≤1}\gamma\subset\{|f|\le1\} joins two different listed root occurrences. A repeated root permits a constant curve; an empty set of competitors has infimum +∞+\infty.

Passing a length bound to a limit.

Let fj→ff_j\to f in 𝒦n\mathcal K_n. If the lower limit of Λ(fj)\Lambda(f_j) is finite, pass to a subsequence on which these infima converge to it and choose rectifiable curves γj\gamma_j with lengths at most Λ(fj)+1/j\Lambda(f_j)+1/j. Every closed unit sublevel lies in |z|≤2|z|\le2: for |z|>2|z|>2, the root factorization gives |fj(z)|≥(|z|−1)n>1|f_j(z)|\ge(|z|-1)^n>1. Constant-speed parametrisation on [0,1][0,1] therefore gives uniformly bounded images and Lipschitz constants. Arzelà–Ascoli supplies a uniformly convergent subsequence.

To retain the endpoints with their multiplicities, list the two chosen occurrences first among the roots of fjf_j, and list the remaining roots arbitrarily. Compactness of the product of nn closed unit discs gives a further subsequence on which this entire list converges. The limiting factorization is ff, so its first two entries remain two occurrences, even if their locations coincide. Uniform convergence of the curves and of the polynomials on |z|≤2|z|\le2 gives |f|≤1|f|\le1 on the limiting curve γ\gamma. For any partition 0=t0<⋯<tM=10=t_0<\cdots<t_M=1, ∑ℓ=1M|γ(tℓ)−γ(tℓ−1)|=limj∑ℓ=1M|γj(tℓ)−γj(tℓ−1)|≤liminfjlength⁡(γj).\sum_{\ell=1}^M|\gamma(t_\ell)-\gamma(t_{\ell-1})| =\lim_j\sum_{\ell=1}^M|\gamma_j(t_\ell)-\gamma_j(t_{\ell-1})| \le\liminf_j\operatorname{length}(\gamma_j). Taking the supremum over partitions proves the required lower semicontinuity of length and hence Λ(f)≤liminf⁡jΛ(fj)\Lambda(f)\le\liminf_j\Lambda(f_j). An infinite lower limit needs no argument. With ff fixed, the same compactness proof shows that a finite infimum is attained. Thus a bound Λ≤2\Lambda\le2 on a dense class gives an actual path of length at most 22 throughout 𝒦n\mathcal K_n. For an open-disc polynomial, choose a containing disc of radius 0<R<10<R<1 and scale: the resulting path has length at most 2R<22R<2 and lies in {|f|≤Rn}⊂{|f|<1}\{|f|\le R^n\}\subset\{|f|<1\}.

For f(z)=zn−1f(z)=z^n-1, the inequality |zn−1|≤1|z^n-1|\le1 implies 2ℜ(zn)≥|z|2n>02\Re(z^n)\ge|z|^{2n}>0 whenever z≠0z\ne0. Thus the punctured sublevel lies in nn disjoint angular sectors, one per root. A path between different roots must pass through zero and has length at least 22 by the triangle inequality. The two radial segments attain that length. The corresponding historical assertion on the closed class is Λ(f)≤Λ(zn−1)=2(f∈𝒦n).\boxed{\Lambda(f)\le\Lambda(z^n-1)=2\qquad(f\in\mathcal K_n).} The lower-semicontinuity argument is proved in the compactness proof.

The displayed universal inequality is recorded to explain the earlier reduction, not proposed here as a remaining open assertion. A counterexample to the original problem would also refute this inequality and, by the same compactness argument, any dense-class estimate implying it. The reduction can still be used for separately specified polynomial classes.
